title: Work through a list

outcomes.can: Trace a loop that builds a running total.
Build a new list from the items that pass a test, keeping their order.
Combine a loop with a division that keeps its fraction, and handle an empty list.

intro: Most programs work on many values at once. This module covers arrays, which have a fixed length, List<T>, which can grow, and the loops that visit each item.

steps.title: Arrays and loops
steps.text: An array holds a fixed number of values of one type. int[] minutes = { 30, 15, 45 }; creates an array of three ints. Positions (indexes) start at 0, so minutes[0] is 30 and minutes[2] is 45. minutes.Length is the number of items. Reading a position that does not exist, such as minutes[3], stops the program with an IndexOutOfRangeException. A foreach loop runs its block once for each item, in order. A variable declared before the loop can collect a result across the runs.

steps.title: Trace a running total
steps.text: Follow total through each run of the loop, then predict the three lines.

steps.title: Follow the loop
steps.text: total starts at 0, before the loop. The loop runs three times: total becomes 30, then 45, then 90. If total were declared inside the loop it would start again on every run. Length is 3, and position 0 holds the first item.

steps.title: Lists that grow
steps.text: A List<T> holds items of type T and can change size. new List<string>() creates an empty list of strings, and new List<int> { 4, 9 } creates one with two items already in it. Add appends an item. Count is the number of items, where an array uses Length. A for loop counts with a variable: for (int i = 0; i < titles.Count; i++) runs with i equal to 0, 1 and so on, and stops when i reaches Count. i++ adds 1 to i. Use for when you need the position, and foreach when you only need the item.

steps.title: Predict a counted loop
steps.text: Read the loop condition carefully, then predict the last line.

steps.title: Follow the counter
steps.text: After two Add calls, Count is 2. The loop runs with i as 0 and then 1. When i reaches 2 the condition i < titles.Count is false and the loop ends, so position 2, which does not exist, is never read. Writing <= there would read one position too far and stop the program.

steps.title: Total the minutes
steps.text: The starter visits every item but ends with the wrong total. Repair the loop.

steps.title: Collect the long tasks
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Build a new list and keep the order of the input.

questions.prompt: What are the three output lines?

choices.feedback: The loop adds all three items: 30, then 15, then 45.
The total of all three items is 90, the array has 3 items, and position 0 holds 30.
Positions start at 0, so minutes[0] is the first item, 30.

questions.prompt: What is the last line of output?

choices.feedback: i stops before Count, so the last run has i equal to 1.
Positions start at 0. The second item is at position 1.

choices.text: The program stops with an error
choices.feedback: The condition is i < titles.Count, so position 2 is never read.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one array, list or loop form each. They do not check a method against empty, single and repeated inputs.
